questions.question_text:
A coin simulator shows tails $9$ times in $15$ trials.
What is the observed probability of tails, as a fraction in simplest form?

options.why: Used the six non-tail trials as favourable instead of the nine tails.

questions.question_text:
A game has probability $0.35$ of a win.
How many wins would you expect in $80$ games?

options.why: Used the probability of not winning, giving $80\times0.65=52$.

questions.question_text:
Two experiments will toss a fair coin: Experiment A uses $40$ trials and Experiment B uses $800$ trials.
Which would usually give a relative frequency of heads closer to $\frac{1}{2}$?

options.why: Assumed fewer trials give a better estimate, although random variation usually has more effect on the proportion in a smaller experiment.
Assumed a fair coin guarantees exactly half heads in every experiment.

questions.solution_text: Experiment B uses more trials, so its relative frequency would usually be closer to the theoretical probability.

questions.question_text: Why do large numbers of trials usually give an observed probability closer to the expected probability?

options.text: Random variation has less effect on the overall proportion.
The expected probability changes to match the observations.
options.why: Treated a fixed theoretical probability as if trial results could alter it.

options.text: Every outcome must occur equally often in a large experiment.
options.why: Confused closeness to expected proportions with equal frequencies for all outcomes.

questions.solution_text:
More trials reduce the effect of short random runs on the overall proportion.
The observed probability usually moves closer to the fixed expected probability.

questions.question_text:
An outcome has theoretical probability $\frac{1}{5}$.
How many times would you expect it to occur in $75$ trials?

options.why: Calculated the expected count of the outcome not occurring: $75\times\frac{4}{5}=60$.
Multiplied by $5$ instead of by $\frac{1}{5}$, giving $75\times5=375$.

questions.question_text:
A biased die is rolled $240$ times. The frequencies for faces $1$ to $6$ are $32$, $41$, $54$, $38$, $35$ and $40$ respectively.
Using these results, how many threes would you expect in $1600$ further rolls?

options.why: Used the relative frequency of not rolling a three: $\frac{186}{240}\times1600=1240$.
Kept the original observed count without scaling it to the new number of trials.
